title: Rules that keep us safe
keyIdea: Some rules are there to stop us getting hurt. Hold a grown-up's hand by the road, because cars are big and fast. Walk, do not run, inside, so we do not trip and bump. Keep away from hot things like cookers, kettles and candles, because they can burn, even when you cannot see steam or fire. Stay with your grown-up in busy places so you do not get lost. Knowing why a rule matters makes it easier to keep.

kid: By the road, hold hands with your grown-up. Cars are big and fast.
Inside, we walk. If we run, we can trip on toys and bump our heads.
Hot things can burn. A kettle can be hot with no steam. Keep away.
In the shop, stay with your grown-up. Then you will not get lost. Every rule has a reason.
adult: This topic, for ages 3 to 4, is about a few simple safety rules: hold hands near roads, walk indoors, keep away from hot things and stay close in busy places. Your child also learns to say why each rule matters. It leads on to everyday safety awareness and to safe choices made without a reminder.

Children of this age keep a rule much better when they know its reason. "Hold my hand" works better as "Hold my hand, because cars are big and fast and drivers might not see you." Short reasons that name the danger (cars, tripping, burns, getting lost) work best. Practise the rule in the real place. At the kerb, stop, look and listen before every crossing, even on quiet roads.

Common mistakes: thinking a kettle, iron or pan is safe once the steam or flame has gone (they stay hot for a long time), running after a ball into the road, thinking a rule only counts when a grown-up is watching, and seeing rules as a punishment, not protection. Young children also cannot judge how fast cars are going, so they need a hand to hold, not just a warning.

In the lab your child holds hands and waits for two cars to pass before crossing. Kit trips when running indoors and gets to the door safely when walking. Then your child sorts a teapot and a candle from a teddy and an apple, matches each rule to its reason, and picks the safe choice in three quick moments.

familyTip: On your next walk, let your child be the "safety boss" at each kerb: they tell you to stop, look and listen, and say why. At home, point to the kettle after it clicks off and ask, "Hot or OK to touch?"

practice.prompt: You are by a busy road with your grown-up. What do you do?
practice.hint: Cars are big and fast. Who keeps you safe by the road?
practice.explain: Hold your grown-up's hand. Cars are big and fast, and drivers might not see a small child.

practice.prompt: There are {n} toys on the playroom floor. Kit wants to get to the door. What is safest?
choices: Walk and step round the toys
practice.hint: What can happen if you run past toys on the floor?
practice.explain: Walking is safest. If Kit runs, Kit can trip on the toys and bump. Walking gives time to see them.

practice.prompt: The kettle clicked off a minute ago. There is no steam now. Is it safe to touch?
choices: No, it can still be hot
practice.hint: Can you always see when something is hot?
practice.explain: No. A kettle stays hot for a long time after the steam stops. Keep away and let a grown-up use it.

practice.prompt: Mia and her mum are in a big shop with {n} aisles. Mia sees the toys. What should she do?
choices: Go to the toys on her own
practice.hint: What could happen in a big, busy shop if Mia goes off alone?
practice.explain: Mia should stay with her mum. In a big shop she could get lost. She can ask Mum to come and look at the toys with her.

practice.prompt: Why do we walk, not run, inside?
choices: So we do not trip and bump
practice.hint: What can happen when you run in a room full of things?
practice.explain: We walk inside so we do not trip on things or bump into people and furniture.

pool.prompt: Your ball rolls into the road. What do you do?
choices: Wait in the road for it
pool.hint: Cars are fast. Who should get the ball?
pool.explain: Stop and tell a grown-up. Cars are fast and may not see you, so a grown-up gets the ball.

pool.prompt: Which one is hot and can burn you?
pool.hint: Which one has a flame that can burn?
pool.explain: A lit candle is hot and can burn. A teddy and an apple are OK to touch.

pool.prompt: Ben says, "I only hold hands by the road when Dad is looking." Is that right?
choices: No, cars are fast every time
Yes, rules are just for Dad
Yes, if the road is small
pool.hint: Are cars slower when Dad is not looking?
pool.explain: Ben is not right. The rule keeps him safe from cars every time, whoever is watching.

pool.prompt: Dad has cooked {n} pancakes. The pan is on the cooker. What do you do?
pool.hint: A pan on the cooker can be very hot.
pool.explain: Look from far away. A pan on the cooker can burn you, even when you cannot see a flame.

pool.prompt: Why do we hold hands by the road?
pool.hint: What is on the road that could hurt us?
pool.explain: We hold hands because cars are big and fast. A grown-up can keep you on the path.

pool.prompt: It is {n} minutes to snack time. You are inside. How do you get to the table?
choices: Run as fast as you can
pool.hint: Which way stops you tripping and bumping?
pool.explain: Walk. Running or sliding inside can make you trip and bump, even when you are in a hurry.

pool.prompt: Why do we stay with our grown-up at the park?
choices: So we do not get lost
pool.hint: What could happen if you wander away?
pool.explain: We stay close so we do not get lost. Our grown-up can see us and help if we need it.

pool.prompt: Which rule keeps us safe by the road?
pool.hint: What do we do at the kerb before we cross?
pool.explain: Stop, look and listen at the kerb, holding a grown-up's hand, before crossing.

visual.caption: Safe or not safe? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: hold hands and wait for the cars, walk past the toys, sort hot things, match each rule to its reason, then pick the safe choice.
